demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
I feel on guard even inside my own home

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel like I don't know myself anymore
I feel isolated and set apart from others
My life has been destroyed by the trauma

issues.item: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
issues.explanation: Physical pain in the same body parts as during the event is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma being an unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one, unless the patient was also physically injured during the event. That makes this item clinically implausible from the provided trauma context.

A global mistrust appraisal is a weak fit with bereavement trauma unless there is some interpersonal betrayal, negligence, or assault-related context. The rest of the profile centers on loss, alarm, and isolation rather than interpersonal threat from other people, so this item is not well supported by the trauma type or the other selected items.

For trauma involving the unexpected death of a loved one, ambulances can plausibly cue the death context and workplace cues may be idiosyncratically linked, but 'People cycling' is hard to connect clinically unless the loved one died in a cycling-related incident, which is not reflected anywhere else in threat, appraisals, or memory. It stands out as a trigger with no supporting context in the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
issues.explanation: The memory profile is dominated by grief-related recall and affective reliving without clear imagery, which fits bereavement trauma. 'Intense shame' on recall is not impossible, but here it lacks support from the negative appraisals, which focus on identity loss, isolation, and life destruction rather than self-blame, guilt, or humiliation. In this profile, shame is insufficiently integrated with the rest of the formulation and trauma type.

vignette: John is a 55-year-old African American man who has come to therapy after experiencing significant distress following the unexpected death of his brother. John and his brother were very close, sharing a deep bond that had sustained them through many life challenges. The trauma of losing his brother was compounded by the suddenness and unexpected nature of the event, leaving John with an overwhelming sense of grief and disorientation. The day of the incident, John had been working at his usual job as a painter when he received a call from one of his brother's friends informing him about the accident. The moment he heard the news, John felt his body tense up; it was as if every muscle in his frame prepared for some imminent threat. He left work immediately and rushed to the hospital where emergency vehicles were still present. The sight and sound of ambulances triggered a flood of emotions, making him feel an intense need to protect himself from further harm. Since that day, John has found it increasingly difficult to maintain his sense of safety. At night, he often lies awake, feeling particularly vulnerable in the darkness, convinced that danger could be lurking just beyond his line of sight. Even inside his own home, where he once felt secure, he remains on high alert, always poised and ready for any threat. John’s workplace has also become a source of anxiety. The sounds and sights associated with his job now remind him of the day he received the devastating news. He often finds himself pausing mid-task, overwhelmed by an intense but vague sense of grief that washes over him without clear visual memories to anchor it. These moments are particularly distressing because they leave John feeling disconnected from reality, as if he is living in a haze. John’s social life has also suffered significantly since the loss of his brother. Conversations about people losing loved ones now trigger intense emotional responses within him, making it challenging for him to engage with others on even basic topics. He avoids these conversations at all costs, which has led to increasing isolation from friends and colleagues. John feels that he doesn’t know himself anymore; the person who was once vibrant and engaged has been replaced by someone who is constantly vigilant and withdrawn. His wife, though supportive, finds it difficult to understand why simple daily interactions have become so challenging for him. They have grown distant as a result, with both of them feeling frustrated but unsure how to bridge the gap. John’s identity feels fragmented; he questions his sense of self and whether life can ever return to something resembling normalcy. John has come to therapy seeking help in navigating these overwhelming feelings. He is most afraid that he will never be able to move past this grief, and that the loss of his brother will continue to overshadow every aspect of his life. Despite his fears, John also hopes for a future where he can find some measure of peace and reclaim a sense of himself. Through our conversations, it has become clear that the unexpected death of John’s brother has fundamentally altered his perception of safety and self-worth. His symptoms are not just clinical labels but lived experiences that have shaped his daily functioning and relationships. The goal in therapy will be to help John process these emotions, rebuild a sense of identity, and gradually reconnect with life beyond the trauma.
